html:
Orenburg is a Russian city on the Ural River, near today's border with Kazakhstan, founded on its present site in 1743 as a fortress and trading post facing the Kazakh steppe. It became Russia's main gate for trade with the Kazakhs and with the caravans of Bukhara, Khiva and Tashkent.

It anchored the Orenburg line, a chain of forts meant to hold the steppe frontier and serve as a base for moving into Central Asia. At its great exchange yard outside the walls, Kazakh herders traded sheep, horses and hides, and caravans brought cotton, silk and dried fruit, for Russian cloth, iron and metal goods. Bashkirs and Kazakhs resented the forts, and the town was besieged for six months in Pugachev's Rebellion of 1773 to 1774, which Pushkin later wrote about in The Captain's Daughter.

In the 1800s Orenburg was a base for Russian campaigns into the Kazakh steppe and toward Khiva. From 1920 to 1925 it was the first capital of the Kazakh Soviet republic, before the new Soviet borders left it in Russia.
